prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Spatial requirements: • It is recommended to reduce motor-vehicle traffic space as much as possible to provide space for non-motorized vehicles and pedestrians. Facility requirements: • Increase slow-mobility signage and pedestrian wayfinding signage to strengthen walkability. • Roadside municipal facilities such as traffic poles, lamp posts, and trash bins should be arranged in a rational manner to preserve the historic and cultural character of the streets and lanes. 12 Comprehensive roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Comprehensive roads are roads that combine multiple road-type characteristics, with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and may include roads with commercial and service functions as well as urban traffic functions. For comprehensive roads, the street design should be targeted according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. Spatial requirements: • Provide street-side spaces for dining and commercial services, as well as leisure and social interaction spaces. Where conditions permit, widen building setbacks to supplement pedestrian, green, and leisure areas. Facility requirements: • Provide continuous facilities, and arrange trees, leisure seating, outdoor display areas, self-parking spaces, roadside temporary parking, and roadside greenery in an integrated manner to facilitate residents’ daily activities. 13 Introduction 1. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. However, the very long straight alignment and wide open roadway may encourage high driving speeds, while no visible crosswalks, traffic calming devices, or protected pedestrian facilities are present.
livability: The scene is dominated by transport infrastructure, with no visible shops, building frontages, seating areas, or social spaces that would support everyday street life.
There are rows of trees and landscaped greenery along the right side, which add some environmental quality, but they are set back from a largely vehicle-oriented corridor.
The bridge-like setting with guardrails and expansive roadway offers little evidence of active public use or mixed functions, so the street appears low in day-to-day urban livability.
sustainability: The visible wind turbine is a strong positive environmental feature, signaling nearby renewable energy infrastructure.

At the same time, the corridor is primarily designed for motor traffic, and no visible bus stop, bike lane, or clearly marked pedestrian facility is present to support lower-carbon everyday travel choices.
aesthetics: The long symmetrical perspective, clean pavement, and orderly lane markings create a visually coherent and uncluttered streetscape.
White ornamental guardrails on both sides give the corridor a consistent edge treatment and a more refined appearance than a purely utilitarian barrier would.
The wind turbine, water edge on the left, and tree-lined horizon add visual interest and openness, although the overall scene remains somewhat monotonous because of the very large expanse of asphalt.
comfort: There is little visible shade over the roadway or edge space, and the open exposure under bright daylight suggests weak thermal comfort for anyone outside a vehicle.
No benches, shelters, or resting facilities are visible along either side, limiting physical comfort for people who might need to stop or wait.
The broad, empty road may feel spacious, but the scale of the carriageway and absence of protected pedestrian space can reduce psychological comfort for non-motorized users.
walkability: No clearly visible sidewalk is identifiable next to the travel lanes; instead, the image shows guardrails directly bordering the corridor edges, which strongly limits walkability.
There are no marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, curb extensions, or refuge islands visible, so crossing this wide road would likely be difficult and uncomfortable.
Although the pavement is smooth and the corridor is visually legible, the street design appears oriented to through traffic rather than walking, with minimal pedestrian infrastructure in view.

Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers

- All Social Groups

- Older Adults (≥60)

 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Data were collected for six hours (8–10 h, 11–13 h, and 16–18 h) on three weekdays in September through December 2018 at each location. The video recording times were selected based on peak expected combined volumes of pedestrians, bicycles, and motor vehicles, with a target of observing 200 pedestrian crossings with interactions from each location. Video data were manually reviewed to identify potential interactions of crossing pedestrians with motor vehicles or bicycles, defined using a conservative threshold of approximately 5 s passing time. Passing time (sometimes referred to as post encroachment time) is the time gap between when the first road user exits the point at which their paths intersect and when the second road user enters it. Due to the time cost of coding interactions, a random sample of 50 pedestrian crossings with interactions was selected from each location (except for the one low-volume location that had only 36), giving 536 crossings for further analysis. These 536 crossings were then stratified on combinations of passing time (<2, 2–3, 3–4 s) and interacting road user type (bicycles, motor vehicles, or both), which were both manually coded (see Table 1). Facility requirements: • Increase slow-mobility signage and pedestrian wayfinding signage to strengthen walkability. • Roadside municipal facilities such as traffic poles, lamp posts, and trash bins should be arranged in a rational manner to preserve the historic and cultural character of the streets and lanes. 12 Comprehensive roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Comprehensive roads are roads that combine multiple road-type characteristics, with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and may include roads with commercial and service functions as well as urban traffic functions. For comprehensive roads, the street design should be targeted according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. Spatial requirements: • Provide street-side spaces for dining and commercial services, as well as leisure and social interaction spaces. Where conditions permit, widen building setbacks to supplement pedestrian, green, and leisure areas. Facility requirements: • Provide continuous facilities, and arrange trees, leisure seating, outdoor display areas, self-parking spaces, roadside temporary parking, and roadside greenery in an integrated manner to facilitate residents’ daily activities. 13 Introduction 1. Purpose of Formulation Under the macro guidance of the “General Provisions,” these Detailed Rules aim at the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads, and are expanded and implemented from four directions: human-oriented, quality-oriented, distinctive, and intelligent. They interpret the refined construction of Suzhou’s urban roads in the form of colorful labels, and create urban colorful roads unique to Suzhou. ➢ Human-oriented: Starting from the users of Suzhou’s urban roads, and taking the public’s experience of urban road space as the benchmark, fully consider the comfort, safety, and convenience of public activities, and realize the value shift from “vehicle-centered” to “people-centered.” ➢ Quality-oriented: Vigorously improve the travel quality of people and vehicle traffic in Suzhou, and emphasize the public space function of roads. Appropriately raise the standards for urban road design, construction, and maintenance, extend road service life, and improve users’ comfort of experience. Reflect a road construction level of high appearance and high standards, with attention to detail and control. ➢ Distinctive: Adapt measures to local conditions, and through the embedding of Suzhou-style elements and the creation of road characteristic scenes, highlight Suzhou’s distinctive urban character of integration between tradition and modernity, so that urban roads become an important carrier and display space for the “Jiangnan culture” brand, and continue the city’s historical and cultural lineage. ➢ Intelligent: Deploy intelligent sensing devices along the roadside, together with cloud service platforms, computing and communication facilities, and through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, realize a travel experience of deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, assist safe driving and autonomous driving, and create demonstration roads with Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. 2.
